vuln_ground_truth.title: Ineffective Shared Escrow Validation
vuln_ground_truth.description: In the `CreatePool` instruction, a constraint checks `pool.config.pool_type != PoolType::NFT` to prevent shared escrow usage with NFT pools. However, this check is applied before the pool account is initialized, meaning `pool.config.pool_type` contains uninitialized data and the validation is ineffective. As a result, a malicious actor could create a pool with an invalid configuration by exploiting the uninitialized state. The root cause is improper timing of validation logic—checking uninitialized memory. This could allow configuration of disallowed pool types with shared escrow, leading to undefined behavior or fund loss.

results.reasoning: The `process_create_pool` instruction mostly initializes the `Pool` state and performs a few parameter checks. However, several user-controlled fields are either not validated at all or only partially validated. This can lead to (a) storing untrusted/ill-formed data that later instructions may treat as authoritative (e.g., `shared_escrow`, `cosigner`, `maker_broker`, `order_type`), (b) incorrect pricing behavior for some curve configurations (delta bounds only enforced for exponential), and (c) cross-component/integration mismatches (the instruction accepts `currency` but silently forces SOL). These issues map to the requested CWE root causes primarily via missing access-control-related invariants on stored keys (CWE-284), insufficient exceptional-condition handling/validation (CWE-703), incorrect calculation constraints (CWE-682), and integration hazards (CWE-435).

findings.title: Unvalidated authority/role pubkeys persisted into pool state (shared_escrow/cosigner/maker_broker)
findings.description:
The instruction stores `args.shared_escrow`, `args.cosigner`, and `args.maker_broker` directly into the `Pool` state without validating any security-relevant invariants (e.g., that `shared_escrow` is a PDA controlled by this program, that it is the expected token/SOL escrow account type, that `cosigner` is not the default key, or that `maker_broker` belongs to an approved set).

While this create instruction does not itself move funds, these fields are typically used by later instructions to gate permissions, route funds, or enforce co-signing. If downstream instructions “trust” these stored keys for authorization or payment routing, a pool creator can set them to attacker-controlled accounts, potentially enabling access-control bypass or fund redirection in later flows.

findings.title: Structured input not neutralized/validated before being stored (order_type and pubkey options)
findings.description:
`order_type: u8` is accepted and stored indirectly via `pool.config` / args without any range/enum validation in this instruction. Similarly, optional pubkeys are accepted without checks for default/null-equivalent values or consistency constraints.

If later instructions match on `order_type` assuming only a small set of valid values, an unexpected value can trigger unintended branches, error paths, or panics. Persisting unchecked structured fields increases the risk that downstream components interpret malformed state as valid.

findings.title: Insufficient validation leads to exceptional/edge conditions (immediate expiry, surprising defaults)
findings.description:
`expire_in_sec` allows `Some(0)`, which sets `pool.expiry = now`, creating a pool that is immediately expired. If downstream code assumes newly created pools are tradable for at least some minimal duration, this can cause unexpected failures/DoS-like behavior for integrators.

Additionally, `max_taker_sell_count` is only set when `Some(...)` and otherwise depends on whatever default the `Pool` account starts with. If downstream logic treats `0` as either “unlimited” or “none allowed”, this can produce security-relevant unexpected behavior. These are edge conditions that should be explicitly handled/validated at creation time to avoid rare-path failures later.

findings.title: Delta bounds enforced only for exponential curves; other curve types may allow unsafe pricing math
findings.description:
`validate_pool_type` clamps/validates `config.delta` only when `curve_type == Exponential` (must fit in `u16` and be <= `MAX_DELTA_BPS`). For other curve types (e.g., linear), `delta` is not bounded here.

If downstream pricing math expects `delta` to be within some maximum (bps-like) range for all curves, an attacker can create a pool with an extreme `delta` that causes incorrect price evolution, integer overflows, or other unintended pricing outcomes during trading.

findings.title: Currency parameter accepted but ignored (forced SOL) can break integrator assumptions
findings.description:
The instruction accepts `args.currency` and comments indicate “support future SPL mints,” but it unconditionally sets `pool.currency = Currency::sol()` and never checks that `args.currency` is `None` or equals the native mint.

External systems (frontends/indexers/routers) may pass a non-native mint expecting an SPL pool, yet the on-chain state will represent SOL. This mismatch between components can lead to incorrect downstream behavior (wrong escrow setup, wrong payment routing, or mispriced routes) despite each component “behaving correctly” in isolation.

findings.title: Potential coding/standards issue: calling `.key()` on a `Pubkey` argument
findings.description:
`maker_broker` is declared as `Option<Pubkey>`, but the code uses `maker_broker.key()` when setting `pool.maker_broker`. In standard Anchor/Rust, `.key()` is typically a method on account wrappers (e.g., `AccountInfo`, `Signer`, `Account<T>`), not on `Pubkey` itself.

If this is not covered by a local trait impl, it indicates a correctness/standards issue that could lead to build failures or unintended refactors later. While not directly exploitable at runtime if it doesn’t compile, it is a maintenance risk.
